issues.legal_issue: Withdrawal of an appeal does not by itself prevent a statutory authority from exercising independent suo motu review over a subordinate authority’s order.
material_facts: The State appealed the Collector’s order and later withdrew its appeal.
The Financial Commissioner subsequently invoked suo motu review under Section 20(3) of the governing Act.
The High Court held that the withdrawn appeal barred the Financial Commissioner from exercising that power.
issues.conclusion: The Financial Commissioner could exercise suo motu review despite the State’s withdrawal of its appeal; the High Court’s contrary view was unsustainable.
issues.legal_principle: Section 20(3) empowered the Financial Commissioner, notwithstanding the other subsections, to call for records of subordinate authorities and examine the legality or propriety of their proceedings or orders. When exercising that power, the Financial Commissioner acted in a statutory capacity independent of the State Government, so a party’s withdrawal of an appeal did not bar the exercise of the power. No earlier cases were relied on.

predicates.land_ceiling_proceeding: The matter arose in statutory proceedings concerning limits on landholdings.
predicates.independent_review_authority: The governing scheme empowered a superior statutory authority to review subordinate proceedings independently of the ordinary appeal process.
predicates.appeal_withdrawn: A party withdrew an appeal concerning the same underlying order before the superior authority acted.

issues.definition: When landholding-ceiling proceedings involve an independent statutory review authority and an appeal concerning the order has been withdrawn, the authority may nevertheless review the order suo motu.

issues.legal_issue: A statutory power exercisable at any time must be exercised within a reasonable time, and an unjustified exercise after an unreasonable delay is invalid.
material_facts: The Collector made the order in January 1976, and the State withdrew its appeal against it in March 1976.
The Financial Commissioner initiated suo motu proceedings in 1990 and set aside the Collector’s order in 1991, about 15 years after that order.
The State did not identify special facts or circumstances that made the delay reasonable.
issues.conclusion: The Financial Commissioner’s order was vitiated by the unreasonable delay and was set aside; the Collector’s order was restored.
issues.legal_principle: Section 20(3) stated that the suo motu power could be exercised “at any time,” but that language did not permit exercise without limit. The power had to be exercised within a reasonable time, assessed according to the facts and circumstances of each case. An unreasonable delay could unsettle matters that had attained finality. Sections 20(1) and 20(2) provided ordinary appeal and revision periods, but the Court did not treat those periods as a fixed limitation for subsection (3). No earlier cases were relied on.

rule.if: land_ceiling_proceeding and suo_motu_review and unreasonable_delay and not special_circumstances_justify_delay

predicates.land_ceiling_proceeding: The matter arose in statutory proceedings concerning limits on landholdings.
predicates.suo_motu_review: A superior authority reviewed a subordinate authority’s order on its own initiative.
predicates.unreasonable_delay: The authority acted so long after the underlying order that the delay was unreasonable in the circumstances.
predicates.special_circumstances_justify_delay: Specific circumstances supported treating the time taken before review as reasonable.

issues.definition: In landholding-ceiling proceedings, a suo motu review after an unreasonable delay, when no special circumstances justify that delay, makes the resulting order invalid.
